OpName: Use: UVEB Curable Coatings, Inks, and Adhesives - Application (non-volatile liquid)
ProcessDesc: Radiation curable coating, ink, or adhesive (liquid, 70% PMN) is unloaded from transport containers --> Dilute and Mix (optional) --> Product is transferred to the application reservoir --> Product is applied to substrate via Roll, Spray, Curtain, or Vacuum coating --> UV/EB Curing --> Cured product incorporated on Substrate/Article (per ESD).
Basis: The October 2011 Emission Scenario Document (ESD) on the Application of Radiation Curable Coatings, Inks, and Adhesives via Spray, Vacuum, Roll and Curtain Coating, provides default values of 250 operating days/year; 548 kg coating/site-batch; and 70% PMN in coating, ink, or adhesive (default for unknown type of product - see ESD for additional details). // Note to user: if you encounter a Mass Balance Discrepancy for the number of sites, uncheck the "Daily Mass Input of Raw Material Containing Chemical" and check the "Number of Sites" option. Press the "calculate remaining two parameters" button to recalculate the daily use rate.
WaterRelBasis: IRER Note: The daily releases listed for any source below may coincide with daily releases from the other sources to the same medium. Per the ESD for the Application of Radiation Curable Coatings, Inks, and Adhesives, raw material sampling wastes are expected to be released to water, incineration, or landfill; due to the lack of industry-specific data, this release is not estimated. It should be noted that EPA expects releases of the chemical from raw material sampling activities to be relatively low in comparison to the other sources of release in the application process.
InhExpBasis: Per the ESD on the Application of Radiation Curable Coatings, Inks, and Adhesives, inhalation exposures are not expected during normal operating conditions for non-volatile chemicals (VP <0.001 torr), but are expected from the spray application of the radiation curable product (see ESD for additional details).
DerExpBasis: Note that the ESD specifies dermal exposures from the following activities: (1) Unloading Radiation Curable Formulation; (2) Raw Material Sampling; (3) Cleaning Empty Radiation Curable Component Containers; (4) Application of Radiation Curable Product; and (5) Equipment Cleaning. Dermal exposure estimates are the same for activities #1, 3, and 5 (EPA/OPPT 2-Hand Dermal Contact with Liquid Model). The EPA/OPPT 1-Hand Dermal Contact with Liquid Model is suggested for use to estimate dermal exposure from sampling (2); this scenario does not present this exposure as the EPA/OPPT 2-Hand Dermal Contact with Liquid Model is more conservative and would encompass dermal exposure from this activity. Dermal exposure estimates for the application method (activity #4) are estimated using the EPA/OPPT 2-Hand Dermal Immersion in Liquid Model. This scenario presents two release scenarios for all workers.
NWbasis: The ESD on the Application of Radiation Curable Coatings, Inks, and Adhesives conservatively estimates exposure for up to 19 workers/site (overall average) for unknown coatings, inks, and adhesives. It can be conservatively estimated that all workers are exposed during each activity.

OpName: Use: Chemical Vapor Deposition in the Semiconductor Industry (gas)
ProcessDesc: CVD precursors shipped to end users in air-tight cylinders (gas, 100%) --> Cylinders connected to gas delivery system --> CVD precursor flows to reaction chamber --> Precursor reacted/consumed (30-50%) --> Unreacted precursors flow to abatement system (50-70%)(per ESD).
Basis: The September 2014 Emission Scenario Document (ESD) on Chemical Vapor Deposition (CVD) in the Semiconductor Industry provides default values of 360 operating days/year; 100% chemical of interest in precursor; and 2.8 kg CVD precursor/site-day. // Note to user: if you encounter a Mass Balance Discrepancy for the number of sites, uncheck the "Daily Mass Input of Raw Material Containing Chemical" and check the "Number of Sites" option. Press the "calculate remaining two parameters" button to recalculate the daily use rate.
WaterRelBasis: Per the ESD on Chemical Vapor Deposition in the Semiconductor Industry, CVD precursors are supplied in stainless steel, carbon steel, aluminum, or electroless nickel coated carbon steel containers (typically 16-gal). Empty containers are typically returned to the manufacturers for cleaning and refilling using custom designed equipment in a clean room environment. Therefore, environmental releases associated with container cleaning occur at the chemical supplier site, rather than at the semiconductor site.
InhExpBasis: The ESD indicates that empty CVD cylinders are shipped back to the supplier for cleaning and refilling. Therefore, there is no worker exposure associated with container cleaning at the semiconductor site. Additionally, worker exposure to CVD precursors is not expected at semiconductor facilities because extensive controls, leak detection, and integrated safety locks are in place for the following potential exposure activities: Raw Material (CVD precursor) Loading and Unloading; CVD Process; CVD Chamber Cleaning; and Chamber Maintenance. Because high chemical purity and tight process controls are critical in achieving the desired deposition conditions and film quality, engineering controls are expected to be used to prevent any process leaks; these controls in turn minimize exposure (per ESD). There is no opportunity for direct, routine handling of or exposure to CVD precursor during semiconductor manufacturing.
DerExpBasis: The ESD indicates that empty CVD cylinders are shipped back to the supplier for cleaning and refilling. Therefore, there is no worker exposure associated with container cleaning at the semiconductor site. Additionally, worker exposure to CVD precursors is not expected at semiconductor facilities because extensive controls, leak detection, and integrated safety locks are in place for the following potential exposure activities: Raw Material (CVD precursor) Loading and Unloading; CVD Process; CVD Chamber Cleaning; and Chamber Maintenance. Because high chemical purity and tight process controls are critical in achieving the desired deposition conditions and film quality, engineering controls are expected to be used to prevent any process leaks; these controls in turn minimize exposure (per ESD). There is no opportunity for direct, routine handling of or exposure to CVD precursor during semiconductor manufacturing.
NWbasis: The ESD on Chemical Vapor Deposition in the Semiconductor Industry conservatively estimates approximately 19 production workers/facility could be involved in CVD. However, none of these production workers would be exposed to CVD precursors.

OpName: Use: Carbonless Copy Paper Coating Formulation and Application (non-volatile liquid)
ProcessDesc: Liquid Raw Material received in Bulk Containers (23% PMN) --> Raw Material Unloading --> Acid Developer Formulation OR Microcapsule Slurry Formulation --> Carbonless Copy Paper (CCP) Coating (liquid, 2.3% PMN) --> Product Finishing --> Final CCP Product (per ESD)
Basis: The November 2012 Emission Scenario Document (ESD) on the Formulation and Application of Thermal and Carbonless Copy Paper Coatings provides default values of 250 operating days/year; 23% in coating formulation; 2.3% in coated paper, and 41,500 kg coating/site-day. // Note to user: if you encounter a Mass Balance Discrepancy for the number of sites, uncheck the "Daily Mass Input of Raw Material Containing Chemical" and check the "Number of Sites" option. Press the "calculate remaining two parameters" button to recalculate the daily use rate.
WaterRelBasis: IRER Note: The daily releases listed for any source below may coincide with daily releases from the other sources to the same medium. Per ESD on the Formulation and Application of Thermal and Carbonless Copy Paper Coatings, on-site wastewater treatment activities at carbonless copy paper (CCP) manufacturing facilities may include ultrafiltration, activated sludge, aeration, clarification (coagulation followed by settling) and powdered activated carbon. On-site treatment creates two waste streams: treated aqueous waste containing a low concentration of chemical of interest and the concentrated solids removed from the wastewater. The treated aqueous waste may be discharged directly to the environment or discharged to a POTW, while the concentrated waste is typically sent to landfill or land applied. Thermal paper manufacturing facilities typically treat wastewater using primary clarification, from which the solids stream is generally routed to a landfill, but may be incinerated at some facilities. Converter sites may not have on-site wastewater treatment and may instead discharge without treatment directly to a POTW. To conservatively assess water releases from a CCP manufacturing site, the default treatment efficiency is not used to estimate releases.
InhExpBasis: Note that the ESD specifies inhalation exposures from Roll Coating and Product Finishing activities.
DerExpBasis: Note that the ESD specifies dermal exposures from the following activities: (1) Unloading Liquid Chemicals; (2) Cleaning Empty Transport Containers; (3) Equipment Cleaning; (4) Coating Operations; and (5) Product Finishing. Since the exposure estimates are the same for all of the activities (EPA/OPPT 2-Hand Dermal Contact with Liquid Model), this scenario presents one exposure for all workers.
NWbasis: The ESD on the Formulation and Application of Thermal and Carbonless Copy Paper Coatings conservatively estimates exposure for up to 90 workers per site while performing CCP process activities; 12 workers from raw material unloading, 30 workers from coating operation, and 48 workers from product finishing. This estimate may also be used for thermal paper manufacturing activities since CCP manufacturing sites commonly also produce thermal paper. It can be conservatively assumed that all workers are exposed during each activity.

Exposures are assessed up to a maximum of 250 days per year per worker.

OpName: Use: Adhesives (volatile liquid)
ProcessDesc: Adhesive received in totes and drums (liquid, 61% - ESD Default) --> Dilute and Mix (optional) --> Load into application equipment --> Automated or manual spray application (some sprayed coating does not remain on the surfaces - it passes into the booth ventilation system and is either captured in exhaust controls or is exhausted into the air through the stack) -> Dryer or other curing method (assessed chemical is destroyed or fixed to the coated surface) (per ESD)
Basis: The January 2014 Emission Scenario Document (ESD) on the Industrial Use of Adhesives for Substrate Bonding provides default values of 260 days/yr; average daily use rate of 51.9 kg adhesive product/site-day; and 61% chemical of interest in the adhesive product (see ESD for additional details). // Note to user: if you encounter a Mass Balance Discrepancy for the number of sites, uncheck the "Daily Mass Input of Raw Material Containing Chemical" and check the "Number of Sites" option. Press the "Calculate remaining two parameters" button to recalculate the daily use rate.
WaterRelBasis: IRER Note: The daily releases listed for any source below may coincide with daily releases from the other sources to the same medium. Per ESD on Industrial Use of Adhesive for Substrate Bonding, trimming wastes represent a potential release point for an adhesive that is not cured or dried. The present IRER does not assess trimming wastes as the default scenario assumes the chemical is cured/dried after spray coating application. If however, the PMN was not cured/dried, the most likely media of release would be incineration or landfill (see ESD for additional details).
InhExpBasis: Note that the ESD specifies inhalation exposures for up to 90 workers from the following activities: (1) Cleaning/Handling Empty Adhesive Containers; (2) Unloading and Transferring of Adhesive Formulation; (3) Equipment Cleaning; and (4) Adhesive Application. Since the exposure estimates are the same for the first three activities (EPA/OPPT Mass Balance Model), this scenario presents one exposure for all workers.  The exposure estimates for the latter activity (EPA/OPPT Automobile OEM Spray Coating Model), is also presented and assessed for all workers; it is assumed that all workers conduct all activities. /// Note: Inhalation exposures to chemical vapors during the latter activity presents a data gap; the PMN is a volatile liquid where the airborne concentration of the chemical of interest is unknown (see ESD for additional details).
DerExpBasis: Note that the ESD specifies dermal exposures from the following activities: (1) Cleaning/Handling Empty Adhesive Containers; (2) Unloading and Transferring of Adhesive Formulation; (3) Equipment Cleaning; and (4) Adhesive Application. Since the exposure estimates are the same for the first three activities (EPA/OPPT 2-Hand Dermal Contact with Liquid Model), this scenario presents one exposure for all workers. The exposure estimates for the latter activity (EPA/OPPT 2-Hand Dermal Immersion in Liquid Model), is presented separately and assessed for all workers; it is assumed that all workers conduct all activities.
NWbasis: The ESD on Industrial Use of Adhesives for Substrate Bonding conservatively estimates exposure for up to 90 workers based on the Motor and Non-Motor Vehicle, Vehicle Parts, and Tire Manufacturing (Except Retreading) industry (default for unknown adhesive). Exposures are assessed up to a maximum of 250 days per year per worker.

OpName: Use: Metalworking Fluid (non-volatile liquid)
ProcessDesc: Neat metalworking fluid (MWF) (liquid, 35% - default, unknown fluid type) is unloaded from containers and transferred to the metal shaping machine trough with other metalworking fluids and/or water (liquid, 3.5% - default, unknown fluid type) --> Fluids are used in the metal shaping machine and recycled back to the trough (spent fluids are disposed) --> Fluids remaining on metal parts are rinsed and dried (per ESD).
Basis: The July 2011 Emission Scenario Document (ESD) on the Use of Metalworking Fluids (MWF) provides default values of 247 operating days/yr; 35% PMN in raw material; 3.5% PMN in the trough; and MWF use rate of 11.42 kg/site-day for an unknown MWF chemical (unknown function and not specified whether water-based or straight oil), where both occupational exposures or environmental releases are a concern (see ESD for additional details). // Note to user: if you encounter a Mass Balance Discrepancy for the number of sites, uncheck the "Daily Mass Input of Raw Material Containing Chemical" and check the "Number of Sites" option. Press the "calculate remaining two parameters" button to recalculate the daily use rate.
WaterRelBasis: IRER Note: The daily releases listed for any source below may coincide with daily releases from the other sources to the same medium.
DerExpBasis: Note that the ESD specifies dermal exposures from various activities (see ESD for additional information). As a conservative estimate, workers were assumed to be exposed during the activity with the highest concentration of PMN (transport container unloading).
NWbasis: The ESD on the Use of Metalworking Fluids estimates a default of 48 workers per site may potentially be exposed to the chemical of interest. Some facilities may also have assembly workers and on-site waste treatment operators, although they would not typically be exposed to metalworking fluids. Large shops may have many more exposed employees.

OpName: Use: Photoresist in Semiconductor Manufacturing (non-volatile liquid)
ProcessDesc: Attach bottle containing photoresist (liquid, 40% chemical of interest - ESD default) to dispensing system  --> Photoresist is applied to to wafer coating (spin coating) --> Soft Bake --> Pre-Exposure (image is applied via radiation) --> Post-bake --> Developing (to dissolve unwanted portion of photoresist) --> Wafer Etching --> Stripping of remaining photoresist from wafer (per ESD on Photoresist Use in Semiconductor Manufacturing)
Basis: The January 2010 Emission Scenario Document (ESD) on Photoresist Use in Semiconductor Manufacturing provides default values of 360 days/yr; average daily use rate of 36 kg photoresist dispensed/site-day; and 0.4 kg chemical/kg photoresist (see ESD for additional details). // Note to user: if you encounter a Mass Balance Discrepancy for the number of sites, uncheck the "Daily Mass Input of Raw Material Containing Chemical" and check the "Number of Sites" option. Press the "calculate remaining two parameters" button to recalculate the daily use rate.
WaterRelBasis: IRER Note: The daily releases listed for any source below may coincide with daily releases from the other sources to the same medium.
InhExpBasis: Inhalation exposure is expected to be negligible for nonvolatile chemicals (VP < 0.001 torr) within liquid photoresist use during semiconductor manufacturing.
DerExpBasis: Note that the GS specifies dermal exposures for up to 18 equipment management/waste management technicians from four different activities: (1) Cleaning/Handling Empty Photoresist Containers; (2) Routine Equipment Cleaning/Maintenance; (3) Change-out of Excess (Spun-off) Photoresist Collection Containers; and (4) Change-out of Waste Solvent Collection Containers. Because the exposure estimates are the same for each activity (EPA/OPPT 2-Hand Dermal Contact with Liqud Model), this scenario presents one exposure estimate for all 18 technicians.
NWbasis: The ESD on Photoresist Use in Semiconductor Manufacturing estimates exposure of up to 48 equipment operators (EPA/OPPT 1-Hand Dermal Contact with Liquid Model) and 18 equipment maintenance/waste management technicians (EPA/OPPT 2-Hand Dermal Contact with Liquid Model) per site (66 workers/site). Exposures are assessed for up to 250 exposure days per worker.

OpName: Use: Automotive Refinishing Spray Coating (non-volatile liquid)
ProcessDesc: Unload coating product containing the assessed chemical from shipping container (liquid, 25% PMN) -> Mix and/or store (optional) -> Transfer to spray gun feed system (liquid, 25%) -> Apply coating to automobile surfaces (some sprayed coating does not remain on the surfaces - it passes into the booth ventilation system and is either captured in exhaust controls or is exhausted into the air through the stack) -> Bake/cure coating at high temperatures (assessed chemical is destroyed or fixed to the coated surface) (per ESD).
Basis: The June 2010 Emission Scenario Document (ESD) on Coating Application via Spray Painting in the Automobile Refinishing Industry provides default values of 250 operating days/year; 1.58 kg coating containing chemical of interest/site-day; and 25% PMN in coating product (see ESD for additional details). // Note to user: if you encounter a Mass Balance Discrepancy for the number of sites, uncheck the "Daily Mass Input of Raw Material Containing Chemical" and check the "Number of Sites" option. Press the "calculate remaining two parameters" button to recalculate the daily use rate.
WaterRelBasis: IRER Note: The daily releases listed for any source below may coincide with daily releases from the other sources to the same medium. Per the ESD on Coating Application via Spray Painting in the Automotive Refinishing Industry, EPA assumes a solvent-based coating unless the chemical use information specifically states that it is to be used in a waterborne coating formulation.
InhExpBasis: Note that the ESD specifies inhalation exposures for all workers from oversprayed coating mists.
DerExpBasis: Note that the ESD specifies dermal exposures from the following activities: (1) Unloading Liquid Coating Products; (2) Cleaning Empty Coating Product Containers; (3) Transfer of Coating from Mixing Cup to Spray Gun; (4) Equipment Cleaning; and (5) Overspray during Application. Dermal exposure from the first two activities is estimated using the EPA/OPPT 2-Hand Dermal Contact with Liquid Model. Activities (3) through (5) estimate dermal exposure using the Automotive Refinishing Coating Equipment Cleaning Dermal Model. The EPA/OPPT 2-Hand Dermal Contact with Liquid Model is more conservative; therefore, this scenario only presents one exposure for all workers.
NWbasis: The ESD on Coating Application via Spray Painting in the Automotive Refinishing Industry conservatively estimates 8 workers per site exposed during application process activities; it can also be conservatively estimated that all workers are exposed during each activity.
